report:
**Conclusion: not convincingly.** Hypnosis may help some individuals feel more motivated or manage cravings, but the best evidence does **not** show that it reliably improves long-term smoking cessation compared with standard behavioral support or quitting without help.

The key evidence is a 2019 Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials. It found the studies were generally small and methodologically limited, and concluded that there is *insufficient evidence* to determine whether hypnotherapy works better than other behavioral support or no assistance; if a benefit exists, it is probably small. This means “hypnosis helps” is too strong a general conclusion—not that it is proven ineffective for every person.  
https://www.cochrane.org/CD001008/TOBACCO_does-hypnotherapy-help-people-who-are-trying-stop-smoking  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31198991/

Guideline evidence is consistent: NICE’s evidence review reports that a meta-analysis of randomized trials did not show hypnotherapy improved long-term quitting, and notes that older U.S. guideline reviewers found few eligible hypnosis studies and no clearly defined method to evaluate.  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209/evidence/ph10-rapid-review-of-nonnhs-treatments-for-smoking-cessation-pdf-392073181532

If someone enjoys hypnosis and can afford it, it could be used as an *adjunct*—not a substitute—for established care. The strongest practical approach is behavioral counseling plus an FDA-approved cessation medicine (nicotine replacement, varenicline, or bupropion when appropriate); CDC says using counseling and medication together gives the best chance of quitting for good.  
https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/about/how-to-quit.html
